authority: Cambridge Principal Examiner Reports for Teachers, 0460, March 2020 to November 2025, Papers 11-13, 21-23 and 41-43. Each entry is a confusion the reports state candidates made.
derivation_policy: Curated by hand from the located error statements and restated in our words. No examiner-report wording appears in learner-facing output.
how_to_use: Every entry earns one MISCON card on its objective. A MISCON card is a DISCRIMINATION: the error, the correct idea, and the test that tells them apart (the test field).

kinds.adjacent_concept: Two different concepts that sit near each other in the syllabus.
kinds.near_neighbour_term: Two terms that share most of their wording or meaning.
kinds.wrong_angle_same_concept: The right concept answered from the wrong angle: explaining where describing is asked, the wrong side of an impact, the wrong scale.

entries.objective_text: Give reasons for contrasting rates of natural population change
entries.a: Mixing up immigration and emigration, or net migration with natural increase
entries.b: Natural increase is birth rate minus death rate; net migration is immigrants minus emigrants. Population change adds the two
entries.test: Is the change caused by births and deaths, or by people moving in and out?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /immigration and emigration|net migration|natural (increase|change)/

entries.objective_text: Give reasons for contrasting rates of natural population change
entries.a: Dividing or multiplying the birth and death rates, or rescaling the answer, when natural increase is asked for
entries.b: Natural increase = birth rate − death rate, in the same unit (per 1000 per year)
entries.test: Is the answer a difference, in per 1000?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /divid|multipl|per 1000|subtract/

entries.objective_text: Describe and give reasons for the rapid increase in the world’s population
entries.a: Giving causes of high death rates (famine, poor sanitation) to explain a fall in population in wealthier countries
entries.b: In richer countries a falling population comes from low birth rates and an ageing population, not from disease or famine
entries.test: Which countries does the resource show, and what drives change there?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /MEDC|famine|sanitation|not relevant|decrease in population/

entries.objective_text: Describe and evaluate population policies
entries.a: Describing how a population policy works when the question asks for its impacts, or the reverse
entries.b: A policy answer separates what the policy does (the measures) from what it achieved (the impacts on birth rate, structure, people)
entries.test: Does the question ask about the measures or the results?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /polic/

entries.objective_text: Describe and give reasons for the rapid increase in the world’s population
entries.a: Treating over-population as simply "a lot of people"
entries.b: Over-population means too many people for the resources and technology available to keep a good standard of living; under-population means too few to use the resources fully
entries.test: Is the answer about people compared with resources?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /over-?population|under-?population|overpopulat/

entries.objective_text: Demonstrate an understanding of the impacts of migration
entries.a: Writing about the migrants when the question asks about the destination (or the origin), or about problems when it asks for benefits
entries.b: Migration has separate impacts on the origin, the destination and the migrants; answer for the one the question names
entries.test: Whose side does the question ask about?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /destination|origin|migrants themselves|rather than the benefits|difficulties for countries/

entries.objective_text: Explain and give reasons for population migration
entries.a: Confusing internal migration with international migration
entries.b: Internal migration is movement within a country (rural to urban, for example); international migration crosses a border
entries.test: Does the move cross a national border?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /internal migration|international migration|rural to urban/

entries.objective_text: Explain and give reasons for population migration
entries.a: Listing push factors of the origin when the pull factors of the destination are asked for
entries.b: Push factors drive people away from the origin; pull factors attract them to the destination
entries.test: Is the factor about the place left or the place chosen?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /pull factors|push factors|attractions of the destination|reasons why migrants had moved/

entries.objective_text: Identify and give reasons for and implications of different types of population structure
entries.a: Describing the shape of a population pyramid instead of the structure it shows
entries.b: A structure answer refers to broad age groups and sexes (young dependants, economically active, elderly dependants) with their proportions
entries.test: Does the answer name age groups and their shares, or only the shape?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /shape|structure rather|broader age groups|single bands/

entries.objective_text: Identify and give reasons for and implications of different types of population structure
entries.a: Writing about general problems of population growth when the question is about a high dependent population
entries.b: A dependent population means a large share of young or old people relying on the economically active; its problems come from that ratio
entries.test: Is the problem caused by numbers, or by the age balance?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /dependent|dependency|growing population/

entries.objective_text: Identify and give reasons for and implications of different types of population structure
entries.a: Reading a single bar of a pyramid, or one sex only, when an age group total is asked for
entries.b: An age group’s share is males plus females in that group; broad groups add several bars
entries.test: Have both sexes and all the bars in the group been added?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /males and f ?emales|male and female|individual age groups|both males/

entries.objective_text: Describe the factors influencing the density and distribution of population
entries.a: Giving consequences of a sparse population (few services) as its causes
entries.b: Low density is caused by physical and economic factors (relief, climate, water, soils, access, jobs); a lack of services follows from it
entries.test: Did this factor come before the sparse population, or because of it?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /consequence|not a cause|services such as schools/

entries.objective_text: Describe the factors influencing the density and distribution of population
entries.a: Defining population density without the area, or describing a distribution by naming places
entries.b: Density is people per unit area (people per km²); a distribution describes where things are and where they are not, using directions and patterns
entries.test: Does the answer relate number to area, or location to pattern?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /distribution|per (km|square)|no reference to area|sparsely populated/

entries.objective_text: Describe the factors influencing the density and distribution of population
entries.a: Naming a physical factor without saying whether it raises or lowers density
entries.b: Each factor is linked to its effect: steep relief makes farming and building hard, so density is low
entries.test: Does the answer say which way the factor pushes density?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /did not link|physical factors|good climate/

entries.objective_text: Give reasons for the hierarchy of settlements and services
entries.a: Confusing a settlement hierarchy with settlement size alone, or goods with services
entries.b: The hierarchy ranks settlements by the number and order of their services; high-order services (a hospital, a university) need a large threshold population
entries.test: Is the ranking by services, and is the example a service?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /hierarchy|threshold|order of (goods|services)|word .services./

entries.objective_text: Describe and explain the factors which may influence the sites, growth and functions of settlements
entries.a: Confusing site with situation, or describing functions when the question asks for the reasons for a site
entries.b: Site is the land the settlement is built on (water supply, flat land, defence); situation is its position relative to the area around it; functions are what it does now
entries.test: Is the answer about the ground it stands on, its surroundings, or its activities?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /\bsite\b|original growth|functions/

entries.objective_text: Explain the patterns of settlement
entries.a: Mixing up dispersed, nucleated and linear settlement
entries.b: Dispersed: buildings spread out; nucleated: clustered round a centre; linear: strung along a road, river or valley
entries.test: What shape do the buildings make on the map?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /dispersed|nucleated|linear/

entries.objective_text: Describe and give reasons for the characteristics of, and changes in, land use in urban areas
entries.a: Explaining why a CBD is changing when the question asks what its land use is
entries.b: Describe land use from the resource (high-rise offices, shops, little open space) before explaining it
entries.test: Does the question ask what is there or why?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /CBD|photographic evidence|high buildings/

entries.objective_text: Explain the problems of urban areas, their causes and possible solutions
entries.a: Answering a strategies question with a generic list and no place detail
entries.b: A case-study answer names the city, describes each strategy, says how it works and adds place-specific detail (a named road, scheme or district)

entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /generic|place detail|lists|strategies/

entries.objective_text: Explain the problems of urban areas, their causes and possible solutions
entries.a: Answering a question on one urban problem (traffic congestion) with other problems or benefits
entries.b: Keep to the problem and the aspect asked: how public transport reduces congestion, not its cost or convenience
entries.test: Is every point about the problem the question names?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /rather than focussing|irrelevant|other methods/

entries.objective_text: Identify and suggest reasons for rapid urban growth
entries.a: Using vague terms (better standard of living, more developed, facilities) as reasons for moving to cities
entries.b: Name the specific pull: more jobs in factories and offices, secondary schools, hospitals, piped water
entries.test: Could a reader picture exactly what is better?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /vague|standard of living|facilities|more developed/

entries.objective_text: Describe the impacts of urban growth on both rural and urban areas, along with possible solutions to reduce the negative impacts
entries.a: Writing about the city when the question asks about the rural areas people leave, or the reverse
entries.b: Urban growth has impacts in both places: in the city (squatter settlements, congestion) and in the countryside (fewer young workers, ageing population)
entries.test: Which area does the question name?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /rural|urban areas|surrounding environment/

entries.objective_text: Identify and suggest reasons for rapid urban growth
entries.a: Defining a rural area by its lack of development rather than as countryside
entries.b: A rural area is countryside, with farmland and small settlements; being less developed is not the definition
entries.test: Does the definition describe the land and settlement?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /rural area|countryside|farmland/

entries.objective_text: Describe and explain the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes
entries.a: Saying that plate boundaries move, or describing the wrong type of boundary for the example
entries.b: Plates move; the boundary is where they meet. Destructive (convergent), constructive (divergent) and conservative boundaries each produce different hazards
entries.test: What moves, and which way?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /plate boundaries moving|converg|diverg|conservative|wrong type of plate/

entries.objective_text: Describe and explain the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes
entries.a: Describing a distribution as "on plate boundaries" with no pattern
entries.b: Describe the pattern: in long narrow belts along plate boundaries, clustered round the Pacific, with gaps in plate interiors
entries.test: Does the answer describe where, how spread out, and where not?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /Ring of Fire|linear|clustered|distribution/

entries.objective_text: Describe the main types and features of volcanoes and earthquakes
entries.a: Mixing up the focus and the epicentre, or a strato-volcano with a shield volcano
entries.b: The focus is the point underground where the earthquake starts; the epicentre is on the surface directly above it. Strato-volcanoes are steep-sided cones of ash and lava layers; shield volcanoes are wide and gently sloping
entries.test: Underground or at the surface; steep or gentle?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /focus|epicentre|shield|strato|lava dome/

entries.objective_text: Explain what can be done to reduce the impacts of earthquakes and volcanoes
entries.a: Using vague terms (better infrastructure, building quality, more developed) to explain why impacts differ
entries.b: Say exactly what differs: reinforced frames and deep foundations, trained emergency services, warning systems, drills
entries.test: Could the reader say what was built or done differently?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /infrastructure|building quality|level of development|vague/

entries.objective_text: Demonstrate an understanding that volcanoes present hazards and offer opportunities for people
entries.a: Writing about benefits when the question asks for the problems of living near a volcano, or the reverse
entries.b: Volcanoes bring hazards (lava flows, ash, gases, lahars) and opportunities (fertile soil, tourism, geothermal energy); answer the side asked
entries.test: Problems or benefits?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /benefits of volcanoes|problems|opportunit/

entries.objective_text: Explain the main hydrological characteristics and processes which operate in rivers and drainage basins
entries.a: Confusing tributaries with distributaries, or source with mouth, or reading the flow direction backwards
entries.b: A tributary joins the main river; a distributary splits off it, as in a delta. Rivers flow from source to mouth, downhill, from higher to lower contours
entries.test: Does the channel join the river or leave it, and which way is downhill?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /tributar|distributar|upstream|source|direction of flow/

entries.objective_text: Describe and explain the formation of the landforms associated with these processes
entries.a: Explaining the formation of a landform when the question asks for a description of its features
entries.b: Describe first what it looks like (shape, size with the scale, position); explain formation only when asked

entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /rather than describe|explain its formation|formation rather/

entries.objective_text: Describe and explain the formation of the landforms associated with these processes
entries.a: Putting erosion on the inner bend of a meander, or saying an oxbow lake or delta forms by erosion alone
entries.b: Erosion is fastest on the outer bend, deposition on the inner bend; the neck is cut through in a flood, and deposition seals the oxbow; deltas form by deposition

entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /outer bank|inner|oxbow|erosional processes|deposition rather/

entries.objective_text: Explain the main hydrological characteristics and processes which operate in rivers and drainage basins
entries.a: Describing the impacts of a flood when the question asks for its causes, or the importance of the river instead
entries.b: Causes (heavy rainfall, snowmelt, deforestation, urban surfaces) come before the flood; impacts come after it

entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /why it flooded|impacts of flooding|causes/

entries.objective_text: Describe and explain the formation of the landforms associated with these processes
entries.a: Mixing up a stack and a stump, a headland and an arch, or thinking an arch collapses straight to a stump

entries.objective_text: Demonstrate an understanding of the work of the sea and wind in eroding, transporting and depositing

entries.objective_text: Demonstrate an understanding of the work of the sea and wind in eroding, transporting and depositing
entries.a: Confusing deposition by the sea with deposition by the wind in sand dunes, or bays and headlands with caves and arches

entries.objective_text: Demonstrate an understanding of the work of the sea and wind in eroding, transporting and depositing

entries.objective_text: Describe coral reefs and mangrove swamps and the conditions required for their development

entries.objective_text: Describe how economic activities may pose threats to the natural environment and people, locally and globally
entries.a: Using vague terms (pollution, smoke, the soil is damaged) instead of naming the threat
entries.b: Name it: soil erosion by wind and rain, a named gas such as sulphur dioxide, a named water pollutant
entries.test: Could the reader identify the pollutant or process?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /vague|named gas|smoke|infertile rather/

entries.objective_text: Demonstrate the need for sustainable development and management
entries.a: Treating sustainable tourism or development as building more
entries.b: Sustainable development meets present needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs: limits, conservation, local benefit
entries.test: Will the resource still be there for the next generation?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /sustainab/

entries.objective_text: use a co-ordinate reference system and give and read four-figure and six-figure grid references to locate places
entries.a: Giving northings before eastings, or taking the figure from a road number
entries.b: Eastings first (along the corridor), then northings (up the stairs); estimate the tenths within the square for a six-figure reference
entries.test: Along before up?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /northings|eastings|grid reference|road identifier/

entries.objective_text: give directions, both in terms of a 16-point compass and as a bearing from grid north of one place from another
entries.a: Giving a compass bearing when a compass direction is asked, or measuring anticlockwise
entries.b: A direction is a compass point (NNE); a bearing is degrees measured clockwise from grid north
entries.test: Degrees or compass points, and clockwise from north?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /bearing|compass direction|anticlockwise|protractor/

entries.objective_text: measure horizontal distances, using a straight-edged piece of paper and the scale line
entries.a: Measuring a straight line when the distance along a road or river is asked, or misusing the scale
entries.b: Follow the route with the straight edge of paper, section by section, then read the distance off the scale line
entries.test: Along the route or as the crow flies?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /straight.line|along the road|scale/

entries.objective_text: recognise essential differences in density of drainage, stream patterns, gradients or sizes of streams in relation to the relief
entries.a: Describing contours or a road when the question asks about relief, or drainage features that are not on the map
entries.b: Relief is the shape and height of the land (heights, slopes, valleys); drainage is the rivers and streams: their pattern, density and flow direction
entries.test: Is the answer about the land surface or the water on it?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /relief|drainage|oxbow|distributar/

entries.objective_text: be proficient in using the key to identify features on the map
entries.a: Using a general term (highway, trees) where the key gives a precise one (national road, coniferous woodland)
entries.b: Use the key’s own category for the feature
entries.test: Is the term the one in the key?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /key|highway|coniferous|coppice/

entries.objective_text: describe variations and identify trends in information shown by graphs
entries.a: Describing a graph year by year instead of the overall trend, or quoting figures without describing
entries.b: State the overall trend, the main change and any exception, then support with figures from the graph
entries.test: Is there an overall statement before the detail?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /overall trend|every 5 year|individual|trend/

entries.objective_text: plot information on graphs when axes and scales are provided
entries.a: Reading a triangular graph along the wrong axis, or plotting on the wrong scale
entries.b: On a triangular graph each axis is read along the angle of its grid lines; check each plotted value against its scale
entries.test: Do the three readings add up to 100%?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /triangular|vertically rather|angle shown|plotted/

entries.objective_text: give simple descriptions of human and physical landscapes and geographical phenomena from photographs, aerial photographs, satellite images and GIS
entries.a: Adding features that cannot be seen in the photograph, or explaining instead of describing
entries.b: Describe only what the photograph shows: landforms, vegetation, land use, buildings, using position words (foreground, background)
entries.test: Can the feature be pointed to in the photograph?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /photograph|could not be seen|in the photograph/

entries.objective_text: understand the terms mean and range
entries.a: Giving one value as a range, or dropping a minus sign or a decimal place the question asks for
entries.b: A range is written from the lowest to the highest value; keep the precision and the sign the question asks for
entries.test: Are both ends of the range, the sign and the decimal places there?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /range|minus sign|decimal|single figure/

entries.objective_text: know the factors influencing the successful design of questionnaires: layout, format of questions, appropriate wording of questions, number of questions
entries.a: Describing a questionnaire in general when a specific sampling method is asked for
entries.b: Random, systematic and stratified sampling are different: random gives each person an equal chance, systematic takes every nth person, stratified samples groups in proportion
entries.test: How were the people chosen?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /sampling|stratified|systematic|random/

entries.objective_text: know the practical considerations involved in conducting a questionnaire: sampling methods, pilot survey, location of survey
entries.a: Giving vague reasons for a pilot survey or for a method ("easy", "more reliable", "cheaper")
entries.b: A pilot survey tests the questions and the method so problems are fixed before the real survey; a method is justified by what it makes more accurate or fair
entries.test: What exactly would go wrong without it?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /pilot|easy to use|more reliable|cheaper|vague/

entries.objective_text: know river measurements of channel width, depth, speed of flow and the size and shape of bedload
entries.a: Describing a float or flow meter vaguely: no measured distance, no timer, poles in the wrong place
entries.b: Measure a set distance along the bank (10 m) between ranging poles, release the float at the upstream pole, time it to the downstream pole, repeat and average
entries.test: Could someone repeat the method exactly from the description?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /float|ranging poles|velocity|flow meter|wetted perimeter/

entries.objective_text: know suitable methods for recording counts, including the layout of recording sheets, instructions and the information required to identify the sheet (time, date, location and name of recorder)
entries.a: Leaving the identifying details off a recording sheet, or counting when timing would remove a variable
entries.b: A recording sheet has time, date, location and recorder; counts at different sites are done at the same time so time of day is not a variable
entries.test: Could two sites be compared fairly from the sheets?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /recording sheet|same time|variable of time|counting/

entries.objective_text: know weather study instruments linked to Theme 2: The natural environment
entries.a: Siting a rain gauge badly (under trees, raised on a table) or not knowing its parts
entries.b: A rain gauge is sunk into open ground away from trees and buildings, with the funnel above ground level; it is read at the same time each day with a measuring cylinder
entries.test: Could rain reach it freely and be measured the same way each day?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /rain gauge|funnel|measuring cylinder/

entries.objective_text: know the illustrative techniques used to present data: line, bar and divided bar graphs, histograms, flow diagrams, wind-rose graphs, isoline maps, scatter graphs with best-fit lines, pie graphs, triangular and radial graphs, dispersion graphs, choropleth maps, kite diagrams and pictograms
entries.a: Plotting bars from the wrong end, reversing the order of pie segments, or shading unlike the key
entries.b: Follow the conventions of the graph provided: the same scale, the key’s shading, pie segments in the key’s order, clockwise from twelve o’clock
entries.test: Does the completed graph match the others on the page?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /shading|clockwise|pie|plotted|misread the scale|order/

entries.objective_text: make judgements on the validity of the original hypothesis or aims using the evidence from the data
entries.a: Stating that a hypothesis is true or false without evidence from the data
entries.b: A conclusion states the decision, then supports it with figures from the results (sites and values)
entries.test: Is there a figure that proves the decision?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /supportive evidence|data evidence|statistics|supporting|no data/

entries.objective_text: refer to the reliability of the data collected and give a critical evaluation of the data collection methods chosen
entries.a: Suggesting "repeat it" or "do it again" as the improvement
entries.b: An improvement names what changes and why it makes the results more reliable: more sites, larger sample, a different time or season, more accurate equipment
entries.test: What exactly is done differently, and what does it fix?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /did it again|repeated their fieldwork|too vague|more reliable/

entries.objective_text: suggest other possible hypotheses and extension work
entries.a: Suggesting an extension that repeats the original enquiry
entries.b: An extension tests something new: another place, another season, another variable
entries.test: Would the new enquiry answer a different question?
entries.evidence: examiner statements located to this topic’s question parts and matching /extension|further|another hypothesis/
